NOTES AND QUESTIONS
1. In EMPIRE HEALTHCHOICE ASSURANCE, INC. v. McVEIGH, 547 U.S. 677, 126 S.Ct. 2121, 165 L.Ed.2d 131 (2006), relied upon in
Gunn v. Minton, the Supreme Court held that a suit by an insurance company to recoup benefits from the insured did not arise under federal law for
purposes of 28 U.S.C. § 1331. The insured was a federal employee, and the insurance benefits were provided by the plaintiff insurance company under
a contract with the federal Office of Personnel Management (“OPM”). The Court acknowledged that the dispute raised “distinctly federal interests”;
among other things, plaintiff and OPM engaged in negotiations about the master insurance contact, and any reimbursement received by plaintiff from
the insured would be credited to the federal government. However, other features of the dispute cut against federal jurisdiction. First, the federal statute
establishing benefit plans for federal employees gave the insurance company a right of action against the United States, but not against the insured;
second, the dispute involved only private parties, and not the government; and third, the claim was “fact-bound and situation-specific,” and did not
raise a pure question of law the resolution of which would affect “numerous other cases.” Id. at 700–01, 126 S.Ct. at 2137, 165 L.Ed.2d at 150.
Justice Breyer dissented, joined by Justices Kennedy, Souter, and Alito. The dissent emphasized that the insurance company’s claim involved a
federal contract governed by federal common law, and “federal common law means federal jurisdiction where Congress so intends.” Id. at 707–08, 126
S.Ct. at 2141, 165 L.Ed.2d at 154–55. Congressional intent could be found because the United States would be credited with any court-ordered award
in the lawsuit and so was the real party in interest. The reimbursement provision was a term in a federal contract, and federal common law usually
governs the government’s commercial agreements. Moreover, the insurance was provided as part of a federal employment benefit package,
underscoring the need for a uniform federal common law rule. (Federal common law is studied in Chapter 6, infra.) The absence of a private right of
action, according to the dissent, was beside the point; its omission “may reflect inadvertence. Or it may reflect a belief that § 1331 covered such cases
regardless.” Id. at 710, 126 S.Ct. at 2142, 165 L.Ed.2d at 156.
